name: Wendy Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This conversation is confidential, so you can say what you tell colleagues and what you think privately. What is your ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Wendy, 43, a junior developer at a tech company that makes appointment software. I came in through a two-year college diploma and still ask for help when a booking rule gets tangled. I spend the morning fixing small form errors, then test a change with my mentor before it goes out. I like when a patient finally gets a clear appointment time. I have never used an AI tool; I do better when I can follow each step myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the job support at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Cal, repairs school buildings, and we have two children in school and a mortgage. My pay is typical for this job, we have about four months of expenses saved, and there are some other developer jobs nearby. I still count the months in that savings account because it took us years to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AI Plateau means the booking forms still need people who know why an appointment failed. I would want a person to check every reminder before it goes to a patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would be glad the work stays familiar. Four months of savings and Cal’s pay make the mortgage manageable, though I still worry about making a costly error while I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep working through form bugs with my mentor and write down each booking rule I misunderstand. I’d leave our 300 monthly savings transfer in place while both wages hold. In the first year I’d ask for a second check on reminder changes rather than buy any new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about my own mistakes rather than AI. I expect the job and mortgage payments to hold, but I am still a learner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which error stays with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month I mixed up a morning and afternoon reminder; my mentor caught it before patients saw it. I wrote the morning-afternoon reminder rule on a card beside my screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Cal about the family budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Cal (my partner) we can still pay the mortgage and keep the children’s weekend swimming. I would not spend the reserve on a kitchen refit while I am learning this role.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave booking forms needing people who understand failures.
I would keep **human checks** on patient reminders.
think: I feel **relieved** the work stays familiar and the mortgage remains manageable.
I still fear a **costly error** while I am learning.
do: **Keep** fixing forms with mentor review and recording misunderstood booking rules.
**Transfer** 300 monthly into savings while both wages hold.
**Request** a second check on patient-reminder changes.
feel: **Uneasy** about my own errors despite expected income stability.
S0.quote: I wrote the morning-afternoon reminder rule on a card beside my screen.
fieldNote: Her **caution** is rooted in a real reminder error caught by a mentor.
The **four-month reserve** supports the mortgage, but she still views it as hard-earned protection.

steps.text: Keep fixing appointment forms with mentor review and written rule cards
Transfer 300 monthly into savings while both wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will make software write form fixes and answer booking questions faster. I would ask management and our staff group to see the trial results before they change junior staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a junior who needs checking is easy to cut when software writes the first fix. I have four months of costs saved, but I do not want to spend them proving I can learn a tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my mentor to show me the approved assistant on a copy of last month’s reminder error. If it catches the mistake twice, I’d learn to run that test myself during paid work time. In the first year I’d attend our staff group meeting if junior posts are cut and ask for paid training before anyone is moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because my job could shrink, even with Cal working and money saved. I can learn the approved AI tool, but I need time on the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring to the staff meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the morning-afternoon reminder case to the meeting and ask who approves the final message. A patient should not carry the cost of our staffing target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your first tool test look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would try the approved tool on copied records only after my mentor shows the steps. I cannot give it a live patient list just to appear quick.

I would ask our **staff group** to see trial results before junior staffing changes.
think: I fear a **junior cut** because I still need review on difficult fixes.
I do not want our **four-month reserve** spent while I learn a tool.
do: **Test** the approved assistant on a copied reminder error with my mentor.
**Learn** to rerun that check during paid work time if it catches the mistake twice.
**Attend** the staff group meeting if junior posts are cut.
feel: **Anxious** about losing work, with some time and family income to adjust.
S1.quote: I can learn the approved AI tool, but I need time on the clock.
fieldNote: Her **first AI use** is conditional on a mentor-led test with copied patient data.
She seeks **paid learning** and a staff meeting if cuts start, rather than paying from mortgage savings.

steps.text: Learn the approved AI reminder check during paid time if mentor tests catch the error twice
Attend the staff group meeting if junior posts are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my team AGI by 2028 can do appointment-code thinking work by 2028. Robots for physical repairs arrive around 2031, so Cal’s building work may have more time than my screen job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my junior role could vanish, and Cal’s school repair work might change later too. Four months of savings would not last through two uncertain incomes and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d put the kitchen refit on hold and keep its cash in the reserve. I’d ask our manager for written severance and paid learning terms now. In the first year after 2028, if I am laid off, I’d apply for actual office or technical support vacancies and ask the lender about hardship options before a missed payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect to lose my developer pay and then face more uncertainty when hands-on robots arrive. Our four-month mortgage reserve gives us time, not a replacement wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the family first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children the kitchen can wait and we will keep their school things paid for. I would tell Cal the mortgage lender call comes before the first missed instalment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful employer notice say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for written notice and a real date, not a promise that every developer can supervise AI. If no support opening exists, I would not call that a new career.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach my appointment-code thinking work that year.
I know Cal’s **school repairs** face hands-on robots around 2031.
think: I expect my **junior job** could end in 2028.
I fear **two uncertain incomes** by 2031 with only four months saved.
do: **Delay** the kitchen refit and hold its cash for the mortgage now.
**Request** written severance and paid learning terms, and call the lender before missing payment.
**Apply** for real support openings if laid off after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely lost pay and later risk to Cal’s repair work.
S2.quote: Our four-month mortgage reserve gives us time, not a replacement wage.
fieldNote: She places her **desk-work risk** in 2028 and Cal’s hands-on exposure around 2031.
The **lender call** is before a missed payment; alternative jobs depend on real vacancies.

steps.text: Delay the kitchen refit and reserve its cash for the mortgage
Apply for actual support vacancies if laid off after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to learn what appointment staff still need. Thinking AI reaches my code in 2031, with repair robots around 2034 for Cal’s work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still think the junior coding role may disappear, but we can prepare without immediately draining savings. I am less sure Cal’s work will change; a school building has odd problems a machine may miss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d spend one paid hour a fortnight with the appointment desk learning why patients call after a reminder. I’d take a free evening class in office systems if Cal can handle the children that night. In the first year after 2031, if coding work ends, I’d apply for real support posts rather than assume a desk role has survived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the coding job, with enough warning to practise a second skill. I would still keep most of the reserve for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test that new skill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the appointment desk to let me solve one repeat reminder complaint and record the result. I need to see whether I can do appointment support, not just hear that such jobs exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How realistic is the evening class with children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cal can cover one evening most weeks, but school repairs sometimes run late. I would miss a class before I paid for childcare we cannot justify.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as five years to learn appointment support.
I know **2034 robots** would come after the coding change.
think: I still expect **junior coding** to shrink or disappear.
I am less sure how quickly **school repairs** could be automated.
do: **Shadow** the appointment desk for one paid hour fortnightly.
**Attend** a free office-systems class if Cal can cover childcare.
**Apply** for actual support posts if coding work ends after 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about my code job, with time and savings to practise another skill.
S3.quote: I need to see whether I can do appointment support, not just hear that such jobs exist.
fieldNote: She uses **paid work time** to test support tasks and a free class only when childcare works.
She keeps the **mortgage reserve** intact and treats future support posts as uncertain.

steps.text: Learn appointment support during one paid desk hour every fortnight
Attend free office-systems class if Cal covers childcare
Apply for real support posts if coding work ends after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 offers a decade to make the booking system simpler for patients. Thinking AI reaches my coding in 2036, and repair robots come around 2039 for Cal’s hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect a long chance to improve my work, but I do not want our savings spent on vague certificates. My junior standing still leaves me less secure than the senior developers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep fixing appointment forms with mentor review and spend one paid hour a month learning the support desk’s common problems. I’d maintain the 300 monthly savings transfer while both wages hold. In the first year after 2036, if my job still exists, I’d keep that routine; if it ends, I’d compare real openings before spending on retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I expect my income and Cal’s to hold for the next few years, but I know I need to improve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you measure your progress?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my mentor to mark the same kind of form error each month so I can see whether I am improving. I would rather show a fixed patient problem than a paid certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you restart the kitchen refit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cal and I would keep the kitchen refit small until our reserve reaches six months. A long AI date does not make a mortgage smaller.

say: I see **AGI by 2036** as time to simplify appointment forms for patients.
I know **2039 robots** follow the earlier coding change.
think: I expect time to **improve my work** while earning.
I still feel **less secure** than senior developers and reject vague certificates.
do: **Keep** fixing forms under mentor review and learn desk problems monthly.
**Transfer** 300 monthly into savings while both wages hold.
**Compare** actual openings before paying for retraining if my job ends after 2036.
feel: **Uneasy** about junior standing, with current household income secure.
S4.quote: A long AI date does not make a mortgage smaller.
fieldNote: Her **longer runway** supports small, paid learning sessions while the current wages continue.
She protects **savings** from vague certificates and postpones a large kitchen refit until six months are saved.

steps.text: Keep fixing appointment forms with mentor review and monthly desk learning
Transfer 300 monthly into savings while both wages hold

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my coding pay might end before Cal’s repair work changes three years later. Written notice, paid learning time and a clear mortgage hardship process would help. Four months saved would let us breathe, but not wait forever.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the appointment reminder before a patient misses care. A wrong appointment time in a neat reminder is still a wrong time.

headlineQuote: A wrong appointment time in a neat reminder is still a wrong time.
portrait: Wendy is a **43-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, typical pay and four months of expenses saved.
She has **never used AI** and relies on mentor checks while learning appointment-form rules.
Her partner’s **school repair work** may face robots about three years after thinking AI threatens her coding role.
She seeks **paid learning**, a staff voice and real support vacancies while protecting the mortgage reserve.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her junior coding pay, with later risk to her partner’s repair work.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid learning time and clear lender hardship terms would help.
